{{Short description|Legal concept}}
{{Missing information|conviction rates and definitions used by many populous countries|date=August 2015}}
{{Criminal procedure (trial)}}
The '''conviction rate''', expressed as a percentage, is the proportion of [[criminal trial]]s completed that deliver a verdict of [[Guilt (law)|guilt]], a [[conviction]], for an offense.<ref>{{cite web |author1=APA |title=Update: Conviction Rates - Association of Prosecuting Attorneys |url=https://www.apainc.org/update-conviction-rates/ |publisher=[[Association of Prosecuting Attorneys]] |access-date=8 April 2024 |date=25 February 2020 |archive-date=8 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240408164011/https://www.apainc.org/update-conviction-rates/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Conviction rates reflect many aspects of the legal processes and systems at work within the jurisdiction; high rates are a source of both jurisdictional pride and broad controversy. Rates are often high, especially when presented in their most general form (i.e., without qualification regarding changes made to original charges, pleas that are negotiated, etc.). Rates across jurisdictions within some countries can vary by tens of percentage points (e.g., across states within the U.S.). In other cases, they are uniformly high, e.g., in China, Japan, and Russia.

While conviction rates can be illustrative of the success of prosecutorial efforts, they also may depict the prevalence of Type I error (criminal conviction where the defendant is, in fact, not guilty). Judge James A. Shapiro and [[Northwestern University]]'s Prof. Karl T. Muth suggest: "When jurors misapprehend how high the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt is, they are in danger of convicting the innocent, the gravest kind of mistake that is called 'Type I error.' When they let a guilty person go free, they commit a less serious kind of mistake called 'Type II error.' In fact, the theory behind proof beyond a reasonable doubt (letting several guilty people go free in order to save one innocent person) actually contemplates Type II error."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shapiro |first1=James A. |last2=Muth |first2=Karl T. |date=2021 |title=Beyond a Reasonable Doubt: Juries Don’t Get It |url=https://lawecommons.luc.edu/luclj/vol52/iss4/5 |journal=Loyola University Chicago Law Journal |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=1029–1060 |access-date=February 21, 2026}}</ref> This concept is not new; a ratio of 10 instances of Type II error (incorrect not guilty verdicts) for each instance of Type I error (erroneous convictions) is sometimes referred to as [[Blackstone%27s_ratio|Blackstone's Ratio]].

==Examples==
===Canada===
In [[Canada]], 2017–2018 data provided by [[Statistics Canada]] indicate an overall rate of conviction of 62% (of those charged in adult court). This is much lower than one might infer from the 3.6% acquittal rate because 1/3rd of the cases are withdrawn (either directly or indirectly via a "Crown Stay") before they reach a verdict. According to Canadian trial lawyer Kim Schofield, the effective conviction rate falls from 62% to approximately 50% if one excludes guilty pleas and deals.<ref name="MoreOrLess">{{cite AV media |people= Harford, Tim (host), and Colin Jones and Kim Schofield (interviewees) |date= 18 January 2020 |title= More or Less: Japan's 99% Conviction Rate |trans-title=  |medium= Radio broadcast |language= en-GB |url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/w3csz3s5 |access-date= 21 January 2020 |time= 5:21-8:46, esp. 6:23-7:02, 7:25-8:02 |location= London, UK |publisher= BBC |id=  |isbn=  |oclc=  |quote=  |archive-date= 28 July 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200728162520/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/w3csz3s5 |url-status= live }}</ref>

===China===
{{Further|Law of the People's Republic of China}}
In [[China]], the conviction rate reached 99.975% in 2022, according to a [[Safeguard Defenders]] analysis of reports released by the [[Supreme People's Court]] and [[Supreme People's Procuratorate]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-25 |title=Prosecutions abandoned, conviction rate record high, and more on China's judiciary 2022 |url=https://safeguarddefenders.com/en/blog/prosecutions-abandoned-conviction-rate-record-high-and-more-china-s-judiciary-2022 |access-date=2024-07-28 |website=[[Safeguard Defenders]] |language=en |archive-date=2024-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240516025959/https://safeguarddefenders.com/en/blog/prosecutions-abandoned-conviction-rate-record-high-and-more-china-s-judiciary-2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[NPR]] and ''[[The Economist]]'' reported overall conviction rates above 99%.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Feng |first=Emily |date=June 25, 2024 |title=China convicts 99% of defendants in criminal trials. Reversing a conviction is hard |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/06/25/nx-s1-4984616/china-convicts-99-of-defendants-in-criminal-trials-reversing-a-conviction-is-hard |access-date=July 27, 2024 |work=[[NPR]] |archive-date=June 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240626011247/https://www.npr.org/2024/06/25/nx-s1-4984616/china-convicts-99-of-defendants-in-criminal-trials-reversing-a-conviction-is-hard |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=July 25, 2024 |title=The nationalism of ideas |url=https://www.economist.com/china/2024/07/25/the-nationalism-of-ideas |url-access=subscription |access-date=2024-07-28 |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |issn=0013-0613}}</ref> In 2016, out of 1.2 million people tried, only 1,039 were found not guilty - an acquittal rate of around 0.08%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Connor |first=Neil |date=2016-03-14 |title=Chinese courts convict more than 99.9 per cent of defendants |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/asia/china/12193202/Chinese-courts-convict-more-than-99.9-per-cent-of-defendants.html |access-date=2024-07-28 |website=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |language=en |archive-date=2024-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240428005731/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/asia/china/12193202/Chinese-courts-convict-more-than-99.9-per-cent-of-defendants.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2013, the conviction rate reached 99.93%, with 825 people acquitted out of 1.16 million people put on trial.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McCoy |first=Terrence |date=March 11, 2014 |title=China scored 99.9 percent conviction rate last year |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/morning-mix/wp/2014/03/11/china-scored-99-9-percent-conviction-rate-last-year/ |access-date=July 27, 2024 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |archive-date=September 19, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230919084504/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/morning-mix/wp/2014/03/11/china-scored-99-9-percent-conviction-rate-last-year/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Several local protectorates in China have set a "zero acquittal policy," resulting in a negative performance evaluation for trials that end in acquittal. As a result, Chinese prosecutors tend to withdraw indictments at the pre-trial stage rather than risk acquittal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Foundation |first=The Dui Hua |title=Behind the Rarity of China's Acquittals |url=http://www.duihuaresearch.org/2015/02/behind-rarity-of-chinas-acquittals.html |access-date=2022-03-29 |archive-date=2022-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308092453/https://www.duihuaresearch.org/2015/02/behind-rarity-of-chinas-acquittals.html |url-status=usurped }}</ref>

===Israel===
The conviction rate in Israel was reported in 2018 to be over 99%.<ref>{{cite web|last=Adv|first=Saul Davis|title=Why is the conviction rate in criminal courts in Israel so very high?|website=Law in Israel|date=6 September 2018|url=https://www.lawinisrael.net/post/why-is-the-conviction-rate-in-criminal-courts-in-israel-so-very-high|access-date=11 January 2026}}<!--Useful article for someone who reads hebrew: http://weblaw.haifa.ac.il/he/Faculty/GazalAyal/Publications/Oren_Gazal-Ayal-Acq.pdf--></ref> Around 72% of trials end with a conviction on some charges and acquittal on others, while around 22% end with a conviction on all charges. These statistics do not include plea bargains and cases where the charges are withdrawn, which make up the vast majority of criminal cases.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Yahav, Telem | date = 14 May 2012 | title = Study: Only 0.3% of criminal cases end with acquittal | newspaper = Ynetnews | url = https://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-4228980,00.html | access-date = 4 February 2019 | archive-date = 7 August 2018 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180807161216/https://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-4228980,00.html | url-status = live }}</ref>

The conviction rate of Palestinians in Israeli military courts in the West Bank is 99.74%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sheizaf |first=Noam |date=2011-11-29 |title=Conviction rate for Palestinians in Israel's military courts: 99.74% |url=https://www.972mag.com/conviction-rate-for-palestinians-in-israels-military-courts-99-74-percent/ |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=+972 Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Japan===
The conviction rate is 99.3%. By only stating this high conviction rate it is often misunderstood as too high—however, this high conviction rate drops significantly when accounting for the fact that Japanese prosecutors drop roughly half the cases they are given. If measured in the same way, the United States' federal conviction rate would be 99.8%.<ref>http://justicedenied.org/issue/issue_67/federal_courts_jd67.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111164454/http://justicedenied.org/issue/issue_67/federal_courts_jd67.pdf |date=2022-01-11 }} 99.8% Conviction Rate In U.S. Federal Courts Can Make Japanese Prosecutors Jealous</ref><ref>https://www.doarlaw.com/blog/2021/04/what-you-should-know-about-the-federal-governments-conviction-rate/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210901162650/https://www.doarlaw.com/blog/2021/04/what-you-should-know-about-the-federal-governments-conviction-rate/ |date=2021-09-01 }} What you should know about the federal government’s conviction rate</ref><ref>https://thediplomat.com/2020/03/carlos-ghosn-and-japans-99-conviction-rate/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220628183240/https://thediplomat.com/2020/03/carlos-ghosn-and-japans-99-conviction-rate/ |date=2022-06-28 }} Carlos Ghosn and Japan’s ‘99% Conviction Rate’</ref>

In Japan, unlike in some other democracies, arrests require permission of judges except for cases such as arresting someone while committing a crime. Only significant cases with sufficient evidence are subject to indictment, since becoming a party to a criminal trial imposes a burden on a suspect; Japan's indictment ratio is only 37%—“99.3%” is the percentage of convictions divided by the number of indictments, not the criminals. As such, the conviction rate is high.<ref>http://www.moj.go.jp/EN/hisho/kouhou/20200115.html Response by MORI Masako, Minister of Justice, to the articles of the Wall Street Journal</ref>

===Russia===
In 2018, the gross conviction rate of criminal cases in Russia was 76%, in 2023 it was 78%. <ref>Judicial Department of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation [https://cdep.ru/index.php?id=79 "Russian judicial statistics data"]</ref> In 2018, 0.25% of court cases ended in acquittal, compared with 0.3% in 2017 and 0.54% in 2014.<ref name="independent">Carroll, Oliver (May 29, 2019). [https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/russia-justice-system-low-acquittal-rate-uk-crown-court-a8935016.html "Russian justice system criticised after acquittal rate drops to 0.25%"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200623071617/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/russia-justice-system-low-acquittal-rate-uk-crown-court-a8935016.html |date=2020-06-23 }} ''[[The Independent]]''.</ref> Jury trials, where not guilty verdicts are more common, are rare.<ref name="times">Bennetts, Marc (August 14, 2017). [https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/russian-conviction-rate-is-higher-than-under-stalin-hj2v7f0bg "Russian conviction rate is higher than under Stalin"]  ''[[The Times]]''.</ref> However this statistic does not take into account the 22–25% of cases that get dismissed prematurely.<ref>{{cite news |title=Российские суды прекращают уголовные дела каждого четвертого подсудимого |url=https://rg.ru/2020/11/01/rossijskie-sudy-prekrashchaiut-ugolovnye-dela-kazhdogo-chetvertogo-podsudimogo.html |work=Российская газета |publisher=Российская газета |language=ru}}</ref> Instead, the Russian statistics consider the number of convictions out of the cases that have made it to the end, not being dismissed in the process.
This is unlike other countries, where all non-convictions, including dismissals and acquittals, are combined into one statistic.

===United Kingdom===
The [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland]] has three prosecuting bodies that cover different geographic areas. The [[Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service]] for Scotland. In Northern Ireland [[Public Prosecution Service for Northern Ireland]] (PPSNI) and in England and Wales most prosecutions are brought by the [[Crown Prosecution Service]] (CPS). More serious cases are tried in a Crown Court, typically by juries and judges, less serious ones in a Magistrates' Court, by magistrates. The figures for 2017–2018 in England and Wales show a conviction rate at [[Crown Court]]s of 80.0%, and 84.8% at [[Magistrates' Court]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cps.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/publications/Key-Measures-Q3-2017-18.xlsx |title=Key measures |publisher=www.cps.gov.uk |date= |accessdate=2020-01-21 |archive-date=2020-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728162529/https://www.cps.gov.uk/sites/default/files/documents/publications/Key-Measures-Q3-2017-18.xlsx |url-status=live }}</ref> In Northern Ireland figures show at Crown Court the conviction rate for 2017–2018 was 87.2% and at Magistrates Court it was 79.0%.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ppsni.gov.uk/Branches/PPSNI/PPSNI/Files/Documents/Stats%20and%20Research/Statistical%20Bulletin%20Quarter%201%202017-18%20(1).pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.ppsni.gov.uk |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906124857/https://www.ppsni.gov.uk/Branches/PPSNI/PPSNI/Files/Documents/Stats%20and%20Research/Statistical%20Bulletin%20Quarter%201%202017-18%20(1).pdf |archive-date=6 September 2018 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

===United States===
{{update | section|date=January 2020}}<!--Coughlan's information is two decades old!-->
{{See also|United States incarceration rate|Incarceration in the United States|Overturned convictions in the United States}}
In the [[United States]] [[U.S. federal court|federal court]] system, the conviction rate rose from approximately 75 percent to approximately 85% between 1972 and 1992.<ref>{{citation |author=Beale, Sara Sun |title=Federalizing Crime: Assessing the Impact on the Federal Courts |volume=543 |publisher=Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science |author-link=Sara Sun Beale}}</ref> For 2012, the [[US Department of Justice]] reported a 93% conviction rate.<ref>{{cite web|author = DOJ Staff | year = 2012 | title=United States Attorneys' Annual Statistical Report for Fiscal Year 2012|url=https://www.justice.gov/usao/reading_room/reports/asr2012/12statrpt.pdf|publisher=United States Department of Justice|access-date=28 October 2014}}</ref> In 2000, the conviction rate was also high in U.S. state courts. Coughlan, writing in 2000, stated, "In recent years, the conviction rate has averaged approximately 84% in [[Texas]], 82% in [[California]], 72% in [[New York (state)|New York]], 67% in [[North Carolina]], and 59% in [[Florida]]."<ref>{{citation|title=In Defense of Unanimous Jury Verdicts: Mistrials, Communication, and Strategic Voting|author=Coughlan, Peter J. |publisher=The American Political Science Review|volume=94|number=2|date=June 2000|pages=375–393}}</ref>

In 2018, the [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] reported that among defendants charged with a [[felony]], 68% were convicted (59% of a felony and the remainder of a misdemeanor) with felony conviction rates highest for defendants originally charged with motor vehicle theft (74%), driving-related offenses (73%), murder (70%), burglary (69%), and drug trafficking (67%); and lowest for defendants originally charged with assault (45%).<ref>{{cite web|author=BJS Staff|title=FAQ Detail: What is the probability of conviction for felony defendants?|publisher=[[Bureau of Justice Statistics]]|date=|url=https://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=qa&iid=403|accessdate=21 January 2020|archive-date=18 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200118111741/https://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=qa&iid=403|url-status=live}}</ref>

There are frequent "guilty acceptance" [[Plea bargaining in the United States|plea deals]] in the United States. That said, the ostensible "conviction rate" may not be accurate because the charges are dropped or reduced.
